Reward points are a separate resource: compare cash paid, top-up cost and another use

Calculate a matched redemption’s implied cents per point, separate actual cash from existing points consumed, and stress buying costs and alternative-use values.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a matched cash purchase with redeeming and buying any missing points

Interactive planning lab

Cash paid to redeem, including purchase of missing points$325
Cash avoided versus the matched cash alternative$275
Comparison after the chosen value of existing points consumed$125

Original hypothetical single-purchase comparison in nominal CAD. The cash and reward alternatives are assumed available for the same product or journey, with identical dates, quality, cancellation terms and all other benefits; otherwise this comparison is incomplete. The reward needs the entered points and mandatory cash. Existing points are used up to the requirement; any missing points are assumed purchasable immediately in the exact required quantity at the entered all-in cents-per-point cost, with no minimum bundle, transfer delay or purchase restriction. That availability is a scenario assumption, not a program offer. The selected case uses 15,000 existing points and buys 15,000 missing points. The chosen alternative-use value applies only to existing points consumed, not to unused points or a second charge on the newly purchased points. It is an authored opportunity-value assumption, not guaranteed cash value or an accounting valuation. Implied gross redemption value is 1.667 cents per required point, before point-acquisition costs. No point-earning spending, annual card fee, debt interest, tax calculation, expiry, devaluation or probability is modeled. Cash avoided is a comparison with an alternative payment, not cash credited to a bank account.

The central idea

A high cents-per-point figure does not automatically mean a large cash saving. Use the cash alternative you would actually buy and count each point-acquisition cost once.

01

Compare the same purchase before assigning a value to the points

A reward can appear attractive when compared with a high advertised cash price. The useful benchmark is the cash alternative the household would actually buy, with the same product or trip, dates, service quality and cancellation conditions.

This example compares an all-in CAD 600 cash purchase with a reward requiring 30,000 points plus CAD 100 of mandatory cash. The household starts with 15,000 points and is assumed able to buy the exact 15,000-point shortfall immediately. No actual program, availability promise or point-sale promotion is represented.

The FCAC guide to choosing a credit card considers reward value alongside fees, interest, use and restrictions. That provides general context for looking beyond the headline benefit. This tool examines one original redemption decision, rather than comparing cards or the spending required to earn points.

02

Calculate implied redemption value before confusing it with cash received

Before considering the cost of acquiring any points, the reward substitutes 30,000 points for CAD 600 − CAD 100 = CAD 500 of matched cash price. Dividing CAD 500 by 30,000 and converting dollars to cents gives about 1.67 cents per required point.

That is a ratio for this matched purchase. It is not a cash balance, an exchange rate offered by a program or a guarantee that every other redemption delivers the same value. The household does not receive CAD 500 in its bank account simply because it chooses the reward.

The ratio also ignores the price of buying missing points. It describes the gross value delivered by the reward’s required point quantity, before the acquisition costs that may be necessary to make the redemption possible.

03

Price the missing points separately from the cash supplement

The default purchase cost is an assumed 1.5 cents per missing point. Buying 15,000 therefore costs CAD 225. Adding the mandatory CAD 100 produces a reward cash outlay of CAD 325.

Against the CAD 600 cash alternative, the household avoids CAD 275 of cash spending. That is smaller than the CAD 500 used in the gross cents-per-point calculation because the reward needs newly purchased points as well as the existing balance.

The cash-outlay bars contain actual modeled cash payments only. They do not add the existing points as another cash invoice. The two alternatives nevertheless leave the household with different point balances, so comparing cash alone does not finish the resource comparison.

04

Give existing points an explicit alternative-use assumption

Using the household’s existing 15,000 points gives up whatever other use those points could have had. The tool lets the reader assign an original alternative-use value, defaulting to 1.0 cent per existing point consumed. That chosen value is CAD 150 for the 15,000 points used.

Subtracting CAD 150 from the CAD 275 of cash avoided leaves CAD 125 of positive comparison value under these assumptions. The last step is an opportunity-value deduction, not another cash payment. It does not establish that the points could actually be sold or redeemed for CAD 150 in cash.

The chosen other-use value applies only to existing points consumed. Newly purchased points are already charged at their CAD 225 purchase price; deducting their price again as another point cost would double count them. Existing points left unused are retained under both alternatives and are not charged to this redemption.

05

A different cash alternative can change the conclusion without changing the reward

Suppose an otherwise matched cash option is available for CAD 420. The reward still needs the same points and CAD 100, and buying the shortfall still costs CAD 225. Its cash outlay remains CAD 325, so cash avoided is now only CAD 95.

The gross implied value becomes (CAD 420 − CAD 100) ÷ 30,000 × 100, or about 1.07 cents per point. After the unchanged CAD 150 chosen value for existing points consumed, the comparison becomes minus CAD 55.

The reward has not changed. The relevant alternative has. Using a higher cash price that the household would not actually pay can make the same redemption appear more valuable. Conversely, a cash option with materially different restrictions is not a fully matched benchmark until those differences are evaluated.

06

Review the two boundary cases: no existing points and enough existing points

If there are no existing points, all 30,000 must be purchased in this illustration. At 1.5 cents each, that costs CAD 450, plus CAD 100 of mandatory cash. Against the default CAD 600 purchase, cash avoided is only CAD 50, with no existing-point opportunity deduction.

If the household already has all 30,000 required points, it buys none and pays only CAD 100 of cash. Cash avoided is CAD 500. At the chosen 1.0-cent alternative value, however, consuming those existing points gives up CAD 300 of modeled other use, leaving CAD 200 of comparison value.

Neither case has a universal answer without defensible inputs and real redemption terms. The matrix makes the two assumptions separate: purchase cost affects missing points, while other-use value affects existing points consumed. When one of those quantities is zero, its corresponding sensitivity disappears.

07

Keep the redemption decision connected to the household cash plan

  1. Use an available, genuinely matched cash alternative.
  2. Count mandatory cash, fees and any point-purchase cost.
  3. Distinguish points already held from points that must be acquired.
  4. State a defensible alternative use for the existing points consumed.
  5. Check the real program’s availability, purchase and cancellation terms.

The model assumes exact-quantity point purchases and immediate use. Real programs can have minimum bundles, annual purchase limits, delays, restrictions or unavailable rewards. Any leftover purchased points and their future use would need a different comparison.

Annual card fees, point-earning spending, debt interest, expiry, devaluation and taxes are outside this single-purchase illustration. They can matter to the broader rewards strategy and should be added where relevant. A point value calculated for one reward is not permission to spend more or carry debt to earn additional points.

The charted comparison separates cash payments from a chosen opportunity value. It does not turn points into a guaranteed financial asset or identify a program the household should use.
